cases.title: Kenya 1989 health cost-sharing fees
cases.point: Nairobi city centre, where the Special Treatment Clinic for sexually transmitted diseases was studied (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Recommended cost recovery in health in 1987 (ISS working paper, Bedi et al. 2003). Wamai links user charges to the Bank's 1987 health financing agenda and to structural adjustment.

lenders.name: Donors (unnamed)
lenders.role: Wamai, citing Mwabu (1995), says fees came in 'amid considerable pressure from donors'.

cases.conditions: Fees for inpatient and curative outpatient care at public hospitals and health centres began on 1 December 1989; children under five and people judged indigent were exempt (Mbugua et al. 1995). No source found quotes a World Bank or IMF loan document that required these fees; the link is the Bank's general 1987 policy advice and donor pressure (Bedi et al. 2003; Wamai).
cases.community: At Nairobi's referral clinic for sexually transmitted diseases, monthly attendance by men fell to 40% of the pre-fee level while fees applied, and only recovered to 64% after they ended; attendance by women fell to 65% (Moses et al., The Lancet 1992). The authors judged that the fees probably raised the number of untreated infections. Mwabu et al. (1995) report a 52% fall in outpatient visits at government health centres (cited in Bedi et al. 2003). In rural Kibwezi, the poorest households used fee-charging facilities much less, and exempt young children showed the same drop as everyone else (Mbugua et al. 1995).
cases.outcome: Outpatient registration fees were dropped in September 1990 after public opposition, about nine months in (Mbugua et al.; Wamai). A revised fee system returned in April 1992 (Bedi et al. 2003).

cases.confidence_note: Harm is well measured, but the IMF/World Bank link is general: sources describe World Bank policy advice and donor pressure, not a named loan condition. The Ministry of Health's own training manual says donors 'worked with' the government to design the fees.

cases.title: Zimbabwe ESAP health and school fees
cases.point: Harare (approximate; fees applied at health facilities nationwide)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Lent two Structural Adjustment Credits (1991–1996) in support of the Economic and Structural Adjustment Programme (ESAP), and helped set up the Social Development Fund to help poor households pay rising school and clinic fees (World Bank OED, 2004).

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: SEATINI says the IMF required the government to cut spending and stop subsidising health care.

cases.conditions: User fee collection was enforced at all health facilities at the start of ESAP in early 1991, with a large rise in fees in January 1994 (BMC Health Services Research timeline). The World Bank's evaluation does not quote a loan condition on fees, but says the Bank could have foreseen that user charges would be hard to run in a way that protects the poor (OED, 2004).
cases.community: The World Bank's evaluators found that outpatient attendance by the poor fell as fees rose and that exemptions reached only a small share of those meant to get them (OED, 1999). Real government spending on health and education in 1996–97 was 10% and 3% below 1990–91, and extreme poverty rose from 25.8% to 34.9% (1990–91 to 1995–96) (OED, 2004). The Bank's 2004 evaluation says health gains of the 1980s were eroded partly by user fees with ineffective exemptions.
cases.killed_note: No deaths attributed to the fees were counted. The World Bank attributes most of the 1990s rise in mortality to AIDS.
cases.outcome: Fees at rural health centres and rural hospitals were abolished in March 1995, while fees at referral hospitals kept rising (BMC timeline). The World Bank rated the outcome of its Zimbabwe adjustment lending unsatisfactory (OED, 2004).

sources.title: Zimbabwe: Country Assistance Evaluation (Report No. 29058)
Meeting the Health Care Challenge in Zimbabwe (OED Précis 176)

cases.confidence_note: The World Bank's own evaluations tie fees and their harm to the ESAP it funded, but no source found quotes a loan condition requiring fees. SEATINI's claim that the IMF required health subsidy cuts is an advocacy claim.

cases.title: IMF wage limits and health workers before Ebola
cases.point: Freetown, Sierra Leone (approximate; the study covers Sierra Leone, Guinea and Liberia)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Ran programmes in Guinea for 21 years, Sierra Leone 19 and Liberia 7 between 1990 and 2014 (Kentikelenis et al. 2015).

cases.conditions: Kentikelenis et al. (Lancet Global Health) report that the IMF required Sierra Leone to retrench 28% of government employees in 1995–96 and that wage spending limits continued into the 2000s. In 2010, as Sierra Leone launched free health care, IMF staff favoured only a gradual salary rise for health workers. The IMF says its programmes in all three countries had no wage bill limits from 2000 to 2014.
cases.community: Using WHO figures, the study reports Sierra Leone's community health workers fell from 0.11 to 0.02 per 1,000 people between 2004 and 2008. Of 36 IMF social spending floor targets for Sierra Leone since 2000, 13 were met; Guinea met 3 of 23; Liberia 6 of 9. By December 2014 the Ebola outbreak had killed more than 6,800 people (LSHTM).
cases.killed_note: No source counts deaths caused by the IMF measures. The 6,800+ figure is the total Ebola toll by December 2014 (LSHTM), not a count of deaths from the conditions.
cases.outcome: The IMF rejected the article: it says health spending as a share of GDP rose from 2010 to 2013 by 0.24 points in Sierra Leone, 0.7 in Guinea and 1.6 in Liberia, and that it made $130 million more available during the outbreak.

cases.title: Egypt 2016 float, fuel and fare rises
cases.point: Central Cairo (approximate); metro fare arrests were mostly at Helwan station

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Approved a $12 billion, three-year Extended Fund Facility on 11 November 2016 (IMF Press Release 16/501).

cases.conditions: The IMF programme included a flexible exchange rate (adopted 3 November 2016), 'reduction of energy subsidies', a new value-added tax and 'optimization of the public sector wage bill' (IMF Press Release 16/501). About 1% of GDP was to go to food subsidies, cash transfers and social programmes.
cases.community: The pound fell from 8.9 to about 18 per dollar; inflation reached 32.9% in April 2017; fuel prices rose by up to 55% in June 2017 (Middle East Eye). The state statistics agency CAPMAS put the share of Egyptians below the poverty line at 32.5%, up from 27.8% in 2015 (Egyptian Streets). In May 2018 Cairo metro fares rose by up to 250%, from 2 to as much as 7 pounds, for more than 3 million commuters (Al-Monitor; The New Arab).
cases.suppression: Police arrested at least 21 people protesting the metro fare rise, most at Helwan station, according to unnamed officials (The New Arab, May 2018).
cases.outcome: Social Solidarity Minister Ghada Waly said in 2019 that rising poverty had been predicted from the reforms and would have been twice as bad without welfare programmes (Egyptian Streets). The New Arab reported the metro rise was part of austerity tied to the IMF loan.

cases.title: Egypt 2024 bread and fuel price rises
cases.point: Cairo (approximate; subsidised bread is sold nationwide)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Expanded Egypt's loan programme to $8 billion in March 2024. Conditions reported include a currency float, subsidy cuts on food, fuel and services, and ending fuel subsidies by December 2025 (The National).

cases.conditions: The National reports the IMF plan to bring fuel prices to market levels by end-2025, with the government free to set the pace. Mada Masr reports subsidy cuts are part of policy recommendations tied to the $8 billion loan. The subsidised loaf rose from 5 to 20 piastres in June 2024, first rise since 1989 (IFPRI).
cases.community: About 70 million people rely on subsidised bread daily (Mada Masr); IFPRI counted 73 million beneficiaries in 2023. Fuel prices rose three times in 2024, with diesel up 17.3% in October (Peoples Dispatch; The National). Electricity rose by up to 50% in September 2024 (The National). The supply ministry says 850,000 people were removed from the subsidy system after June 2026 (AFP via Kuwait Times).
cases.outcome: Prime Minister Madbouly said the government would review IMF targets and timelines 'if people cannot bear it' (The National, October 2024). Further removals from ration lists were planned for 2027 (Kuwait Times).

cases.title: Jordan 2018 income tax protests
cases.point: Fourth Circle near the Prime Ministry in Amman, where nightly protests gathered (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Signed a $700 million, 36-month Extended Fund Facility with Jordan in 2016. Passing the income tax law was needed before the programme's second review could go ahead (Jordan Times).

cases.conditions: The draft income tax law of May 2018 cut the family exemption from JD24,000 to JD16,000 a year, raised brackets from three to five and raised taxes on industry and banks (MERIP). Arab News says a general sales tax rise and the end of bread subsidies earlier in 2018 were IMF-driven. The final law (late 2018) set thresholds at JD20,000 for families and JD10,000 for individuals (Jordan Times).
cases.community: Earlier 2018 measures raised sales tax on 164 basic goods to 10%; bread prices roughly doubled and electricity rose 55% from January (MERIP). Al Jazeera reports the share of citizens paying income tax would rise from 4.5% to 10%. Unemployment among Jordanians was 18.4% (Department of Statistics, via Arab News).
cases.suppression: Riot police fired tear gas to keep protesters from the prime minister's office. Police said 60 people were detained and 42 security officers injured (Arab News). Gendarmerie blocked the Fourth Circle on 1 June (MERIP).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: Thirty-three unions struck on 30 May. Prime Minister Hani Mulki resigned on 4 June; his successor Omar al-Razzaz withdrew the draft on 7 June (MERIP). A revised law passed in late 2018 and took effect in 2019 (Jordan Times).

cases.title: Tunisia 2018–19 public sector wage strikes
cases.point: Tunis (approximate); the UGTT union called nationwide walkouts

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Agreed a loan programme worth about $2.8 billion in December 2016. In 2017 staff called Tunisia's wage bill 'among the highest in the world' and pressed to bring it toward 12% of GDP by 2020 (IMF Press Release 17/319).

cases.conditions: The IMF called for containing the public wage bill toward 12% of GDP by 2020 (IMF, August 2017). Reuters reported IMF pressure to freeze public sector wages and a government target of 12.5% of GDP by 2020, down from 15.5% (Al Jazeera, 2019).
cases.community: About 650,000 public sector workers struck on 22 November 2018, closing schools, universities and ministries; hospitals ran emergency staff only (Al Jazeera; Reuters via Egypt Independent). The state Institute of Strategic Studies said real purchasing power fell 40% since 2014 (Al Jazeera). A 670,000-strong civil service strike followed in January 2019.
cases.outcome: UGTT head Noureddine Taboubi said the decision lay with the IMF, not the government. Government spokesman Iyad Dahmani said lenders including the IMF had threatened to stop financing without reforms (Reuters via Egypt Independent).

cases.title: Ghana 2015 hiring freeze and unposted nurses
cases.point: Accra, seat of the ministries of health and finance (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Approved a three-year, $918 million Extended Credit Facility on 3 April 2015, relying on wage restraint, payroll clean-up and 'limited net hiring' (IMF Press Release 15/159).

cases.conditions: The IMF's first review in August 2015 described a 'net hiring freeze' with exemptions for health and education (IMF Press Release 15/393). 3News reported the IMF wanted the wage bill cut to about 35% of tax revenue, from about 50% in 2014.
cases.community: Over 2,000 trained nurses and midwives who finished national service were left waiting for posts; the Finance Ministry said there was no money (3News, July 2015). A 2021 ActionAid report says the hiring freeze and cap on wage rises limited hiring of teachers, nurses and doctors (Daily Graphic).
cases.outcome: The Coalition of Unemployed Nurses and Midwives threatened demonstrations; the health minister asked for time without a deadline (3News). ActionAid in 2021 called for an end to wage bill constraints (Daily Graphic).

cases.title: Zambia 2004 wage freeze and unhired teachers
cases.point: Lusaka (approximate; rural schools were hit hardest)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Agreed a wage cap with the government in 2003 after an unbudgeted pay rise and housing allowance; HIPC debt relief depended on meeting programme benchmarks (IRIN 2005; IMF letter 2004).

cases.conditions: State employee wages were frozen for six months from February 2004 as part of IMF and World Bank conditions (IRIN 2005). Oxfam said IMF conditions capped public wages at 8% of GDP (IRIN 2004). The IMF says teachers, doctors and nurses were exempted from the hiring freeze in its November 2002 policy memorandum.
cases.community: Oxfam counted a shortage of about 9,000 teachers while around 12,000 trained teachers could not be put on the payroll because of a spending ceiling (IRIN 2004). The teachers' union said some rural pupils saw no teacher during 2004. An income tax rise of up to 40% hit about 495,000 workers (IRIN 2005).
cases.outcome: Workers struck against the tax rise and wage cap; the ZCTU said 90% of public workers joined (IRIN 2005). The Netherlands gave $10 million to pay off retiring teachers so about 7,000 could be replaced (IMF letter).

cases.confidence_note: Oxfam and teachers' unions blame IMF spending ceilings. The IMF says 'at no time' did its policies bar hiring teachers, and blames pay rises and unpaid retirement benefits.

cases.title: Zambia 2022 fuel subsidy removal
cases.point: Lusaka (approximate; fuel prices are set nationally)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Approved a 38-month, $1.3 billion Extended Credit Facility on 31 August 2022, with the aim to 'Eliminate regressive fuel subsidies' (IMF Press Release 22/297).

cases.conditions: The IMF programme called for ending fuel subsidies and making the farm input subsidy more efficient (IMF Press Release 22/297). ActionAid Zambia reports monthly cost-based fuel price reviews, VAT and excise on fuel reinstated by September 2022 on IMF advice, and a benchmark to move the farm input programme to e-vouchers in 33 districts.
cases.community: Petrol prices rose 58.7% and diesel 39% between September 2022 and February 2024; inflation was 13.2% in January 2024 (ActionAid Zambia). ActionAid estimates each 2-kwacha rise per litre cuts average real income by 2.4%, hitting low-income and women-headed households hardest. The health service had about 60,000 unfilled posts (ActionAid Zambia).
cases.outcome: Fuel prices are now reviewed every 30 days. ActionAid Zambia called for relief on the cost of living.

cases.title: Guinea 2006 fuel price strikes and killings
cases.point: Conakry (approximate); killings were also reported in Labé

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Ran a Staff-Monitored Program from 2005. In January 2006 its directors advised that petroleum prices move in line with world prices (IMF PIN 06/07).

cases.conditions: The May 2005 letter of intent fixed the 2005 wage bill at 2.9% of GDP and recorded the 1 March 2005 move to a market exchange rate (IMF). IMF directors advised letting fuel prices follow world prices (IMF, 2006). IRIN reports the May 2006 fuel price rises were made in line with IMF policy to end fuel subsidies.
cases.community: The Guinean franc lost 38% of its value after March 2005; inflation reached about 28–30% (IRIN). A graduate civil servant's monthly pay fell 40% in value to about US$40, while a 50-kg sack of rice cost over US$25 (IRIN, June 2006).
cases.suppression: During the June 2006 strike, security forces shot protesters, many of them students denied exams. HRW gathered accounts of 13 killings in Conakry and Labé, two rapes, and beatings in police custody with release only on bribes. Earlier, in March 2006, the president's guards fired on youths, killing a bystander (IRIN).
cases.killed_note: Official toll 11; local civil society groups counted 21 killed by security force gunfire (Human Rights Watch). Mail & Guardian reported at least 18 dead and 83 wounded from witnesses and hospitals.
cases.outcome: The March 2006 strike won a promise of 30% civil service pay rises and a minimum wage (IRIN). Unions kept demanding lower fuel and rice prices; larger strikes followed in January 2007.

cases.title: Malawi 2023 kwacha devaluation
cases.point: Lilongwe, seat of the Reserve Bank of Malawi (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Approved a 48-month, $178 million Extended Credit Facility on 15 November 2023, six days after the devaluation (IMF Country Report 23/375; Bloomberg).

cases.conditions: As a prior action, the central bank changed its foreign exchange operations so dealers could trade at 'freely negotiated rates', and committed to greater exchange rate flexibility (IMF Country Report 23/375). On 9 November 2023 the kwacha was devalued 44%, from 1,180 to 1,700 per dollar (Bloomberg). The IMF later called it a difficult decision that 'imposed short-term hardship' (IMF, 2024).
cases.community: Annual inflation rose from 26.9% in October to 33.1% in November 2023, and food inflation from 34.5% to 41.7% (National Statistical Office, via The Nation). ActionAid Malawi says the devaluation pushed most people into extreme poverty and that relief covered only four cities (AllAfrica). Over 70% of Malawians lived below $2.15 a day (IMF).
cases.outcome: President Chakwera spoke of 'the agony of the painful corrections' and asked for wage and tax relief (Bloomberg via Yahoo). The IMF called for a market-clearing exchange rate on an ongoing basis (The Nation).

cases.title: Ethiopia 2024 birr float and fuel price rises
cases.point: Addis Ababa (approximate; fuel prices are set nationally)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Approved a four-year, $3.4 billion Extended Credit Facility on 29 July 2024 (IMF Press Release 24/291).

cases.conditions: The programme moves Ethiopia to a market-determined exchange rate and says 'temporary subsidies on fuel and fertilizers' are to be unwound gradually, while raising the budget for the PSNP cash transfer (IMF Press Release 24/291). AllAfrica reports the trade ministry's fuel price plan was referred to in the government's agreement with the IMF.
cases.community: The birr went from 57 to about 112–114 per dollar within ten days of the float, and fuel prices nearly doubled in birr terms (Health Poverty Action). In October 2024 benzene rose from 82.60 to 91.14 birr a litre and diesel to 90.28, with a target near 117 birr by October 2025 (AllAfrica). Health Poverty Action reports teachers, nurses and doctors struggling with rent and food costs.
cases.outcome: The government announced quarterly fuel price rises until subsidies end (AllAfrica).

cases.title: Ghana 1985 hospital fees (cash and carry)
cases.point: Accra (approximate; fees applied at public facilities nationwide)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Coleman (Harvard, 1997) says user fees were usually started at the Bank's urging and the Bank's 1987 'Agenda for Health Reform' backed cost recovery.

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Ghana's government had adopted the World Bank/IMF Structural Adjustment Program with its conditions (Coleman, 1997).

cases.conditions: The 1985 Hospital Fee Regulation (LI 1313) set fees by facility level, aimed at full recovery of drug costs, with exemptions for some groups (Coleman, 1997). Peoples Dispatch describes the 'cash and carry' system as part of spending cuts under the joint IMF–World Bank adjustment programme.
cases.community: Waddington and Enyimayew (1989), cited by Coleman, found a sharp fall in use of outpatient care after the 1985 fees. Peoples Dispatch reports use of state health care fell by about 60% and fees rose 800% to 1,000% in 1986. Exemptions were largely not followed (Coleman).
cases.outcome: Facilities came to keep all fee revenue and charges rose well above 1985 levels (Coleman, 1997).
